candidates.topic: Minimum Node version and runtime dependencies

reference.quote:
## Runtime

The package requires Node.js >=24. Its runtime dependencies are `@ast-grep/cli` and `yaml`.

target.quote:
## Code

- Node 24 or later, ESM (`"type": "module"`). This is a floor this package
  chooses, above what Node still supports: 22 is alive until April 2027.
  The suite's own floor is lower -- `--experimental-strip-types` arrived in
  22.6 -- so a test passing says nothing about `engines`.
- Two runtime dependencies, `yaml` and `@ast-grep/cli`, and adding a third
  is a decision, not a detail: `src/` runs from source in CI and in the git
  hooks, so anything installed here executes in the same process that holds
  the API key.
- `dist/` is built, never committed.

candidates.topic: The current default model versus explicit model overrides

reference.quote:
## Default model

The default model is `jev-1.14.0`. Explicit CLI, configuration and environment overrides still apply.

target.quote:
## Model recommendation

The default is pinned to `jev-1.14.0`, the
[current stable release](https://docs.typesafe.ai/models), so a moving alias cannot
silently change answers at fitted cutoffs. Override it with `--model`, config's
`model:`, or `JEV_LINT_MODEL`. `--model jev-latest` follows future stable releases.

Jev is the recommended model for normal linting. The shipped rules and cutoffs
are calibrated for Jev, and it performed best at those cutoffs in the
[81-suite fixture comparison](docs/clef-evaluation.md#live-results-2026-10-02).

Cloudflare Clef and Clef-flash are optional experimental models for comparison
from a repository checkout. `just clef-plan` previews the requests and cost;
`just clef-eval` runs the comparison with Cloudflare credentials. See the
[evaluation guide](docs/clef-evaluation.md) for setup, recorded results and
the limits of fitting new cutoffs on the same fixtures.

candidates.topic: The complete local CI pipeline and its final stage

reference.quote:
## CI

The local CI command is `npm run ci`. Its complete package script is:

```sh
npm run skills:check && npm run typecheck && npm test && npm run build && npm run eval:replay && npm run eval:adoption && npm run docs:facts:check && npm run eval:documents && npm run docs:replay
```

target.quote:
## Build contract

`"type": "module"`, so plain `.ts` files are ESM. Three settings keep one source
tree runnable three ways — through `tsc` for the published build, through
`node --experimental-strip-types` for development, and from `dist/` once
installed:

- `allowImportingTsExtensions` + `rewriteRelativeImportExtensions` — source
  imports `./x.ts`, the emit rewrites to `./x.js`.
- `erasableSyntaxOnly` — anything TypeScript cannot simply erase is a compile
  error here, so the stripped-types run and the compiled run cannot diverge.

`package.json` ships compiled `dist`, rule YAML files and public documentation.
It does not publish rule fixtures or accepted rule baselines; replaying those
requires a repository checkout. [Project facts](../project-facts.md#package-contents)
is generated from the actual export map and publish allowlist.

`npm run ci` checks the skill link, types, tests, build, rule baseline replay,
adoption evaluation, generated documentation facts, document evaluation replay,
and finally the committed documentation snapshot replay. None needs an API key.
The complete command is generated in [project facts](../project-facts.md#ci).
Rule replay fails when an accepted decision regresses or the rule question
changes. Document replay fails on contradictions, omissions or stale source,
manifest and question digests; a live refresh is required after input changes.

reference.quote:
## CI

The local CI command is `npm run ci`. Its complete package script is:

```sh
npm run skills:check && npm run typecheck && npm test && npm run build && npm run eval:replay && npm run eval:adoption && npm run docs:facts:check && npm run eval:documents && npm run docs:replay
```

target.quote:
## Rules and their evals

- A rule is `rules/<language>/<id>/rule.yml` with `fixtures/`, `expect.yml`
  (labelled defects and cleans), and an accepted `baseline.json` beside it.
  `last.json` is untracked. `jev-lint eval rules/<language>/<id> --repeat 3`
  runs it; `--accept` promotes the
  run; `npm run ci` includes `jev-lint eval --replay`, which fails on a case
  that was right when accepted and is wrong now, or on a rule whose question
  changed since its baseline. The case files carry NO `// DEFECT` /
  `// CLEAN` markers: those sat inside the file the model was shown, and the
  fits they produced were better than the rules (six fell when they came
  out). Editing a case file means shifting the labels below the edit; the
  test suite fails on a label no subject sits on.
- Each suite labels only its own rule. `tools/arms.ts` and
  `tools/grouping.ts` run every rule over every suite's cases
  (`evalCorpus`), where another rule's answer on a suite's file is clean by
  default -- a defect for rule A in rule B's cases is B's false positive
  until labelled.
- A fixture file named for the rule it exercises carries
  `// jev-lint-ignore-file module-name-describes-contents` on line 1, above
  its imports, so the module rule does not judge a name that was never a
  claim about the exports.
- A new shipped rule needs its own fixtures with hard cleans, `gaps`,
  repeated `eval`, a report with a verdict, and a pass over unseen code
  before it enters `rules/<language>/<id>/` with an accepted baseline.
- Any change to a shipped rule's `ask`, `criteria`, `note`, matcher,
  `subject` or `state` is a new question: `jev-lint eval --replay` refuses
  the old baseline until you run `jev-lint eval rules/<language>/<id> --repeat 3`,
  read the result, and `--accept` it. Commit the baseline with the rule.
- `tools/arms.ts` measures every arm per rule over every suite's cases
  (five arms, two passes, about twenty cents). Re-run it after changing a matcher or splitting a rule; the
  shipped `state:` choices are measurements, not preferences.
- `just docs-facts` regenerates current catalog, runtime, model and CI facts.
  `just docs-check --record .jev-lint/documents-baseline.json` refreshes the
  semantic documentation comparisons; `just docs-replay` validates that record
  offline. Refresh after changing a registered source or comparison selector.
- Figures quoted in `README.md`, `docs/reference.md` and `docs/deepdive.md`
  are measured. Change the measurement and the figure together, or neither.

candidates.topic: Whether a newly shipped rule requires labelled fixtures and an accepted baseline

reference.quote:
## Rules

- A rule lives at `rules/<lang>/<id>/rule.yml`, with `fixtures/` beside it,
  an `expect.yml` labelling them, and the accepted `baseline.json`. A rule
  file anywhere else has no fixtures and no tier, and that is a different
  thing.
- A rule ships with a cutoff that was fitted, and the `threshold:` carries a
  comment naming the run it came from, what the defects answered, where the
  cleans topped out, and the pass-to-pass spread. A guessed cutoff is
  written `threshold: 0.7  # uncalibrated` and does not ship that way.
- `baseline.json` is committed; `last.json` is not — `.gitignore` already
  says so. A change to what a rule asks or matches needs a newly accepted
  baseline. Renaming `at:` to `threshold:` without changing the number
  preserves the normalized rule and its accepted answers.
- The same `id` under two language directories carries the same `ask:`,
  `criteria:` and `note:`. Change one and change the other, or say in
  `divergent:` why that language's failure is shaped differently.
- Never write a rule a compiler, type checker or conventional linter can
  decide. Those belong to the existing tools.

target.quote:
### Evals: the cases a rule ships with

A cutoff is fitted, not chosen, and a rule is only as good as the cases it
is measured on. Each rule directory carries them, under its language:

```
rules/typescript/catch-hides-failure/
  rule.yml                 one language; a Rust twin goes under rules/rust/
  fixtures/handlers.ts     code that reads like real code -- no markers in it
  expect.yml               fixtures/handlers.ts: [{ line: 12, label: bad, window: 0, reason: "..." }]
  baseline.json            the accepted run: answers, cutoffs, the rule's draft hash
```

The language directory admits only its own grammars (`typescript` admits
the ECMAScript four), so one language's matcher cannot land in another's
file. The same id under two languages is one rule in two languages: it
shares the id in findings and `--threshold`, and the loader warns if the two
copies of the sentence drift. Every shipped rule, in every language, requires
labelled fixtures, an `expect.yml` and an accepted `baseline.json`.
`typescript` and `rust` are first tier; the remaining language packs are
calibrated to the same standard without that support promise. Uncalibrated
experiments stay outside the shipped `rules/<language>/<id>/` catalog.

Expectations live in `expect.yml` and never in the code: a `// DEFECT: named seconds,
holds milliseconds` above a case is inside the file the model is shown, and
the fit then measures the label instead of the rule — which is how this
repository's own corpus once claimed 22 rules at 1.00/1.00 and had 17.
Put in the hard clean cases, the ones a lazy rule would flag.

And put them **near the cutoff**. A corpus of obvious defects and obvious
cleans scores 1.00 on both axes and measures nothing: the rule could drift a
quarter of the way across its scale and no number would move. `jev-lint eval`
refuses a suite in that state — and equally one whose nearest case sits closer
to the cutoff than that case's own pass-to-pass spread, where the score is
decided by the run rather than by the rule. A rule for which this is a genuine
property rather than a lazy corpus says so in `inconclusive:`, naming what was
tried and what it answered; a declaration on a suite that does not need one is
an error.

```bash
jev-lint eval rules/typescript/catch-hides-failure --repeat 3   # ask 3 times, score at the shipped cutoff
jev-lint eval rules/typescript/catch-hides-failure --accept     # ...and make that run the baseline
jev-lint eval --replay                                 # every rule, no requests: the CI gate
```

The score is at the rule's **shipped** cutoff on the mean of the passes —
does the rule as it ships still get its cases right — with the fitted cutoff
printed beside it, not used. `--replay` re-scores every baseline at the
current cutoffs without a request and fails on a case that was right when
the baseline was accepted and is wrong now, or on a rule whose sentence,
criteria, matcher, subject or state changed since: those answers were to a
different question, and the eval has to be run and accepted again. This
repository's `npm run ci` includes it alongside adoption and documentation checks.

Every field, `score` versus `noul`, the state arms with their measurements,
and sharing one sentence across grammars are in
[reference.md](reference.md#rule-fields).

candidates.topic: The distinction between accepted-findings baselines and verdict caches

reference.quote:
## Baselines and caches

A verdict cache stores reusable model answers. The ordinary CLI cache is
`.jev-lint/baseline.json`; the strict audit cache also binds the entire request,
tenant, repository, endpoint, model deployment and selected policy. Cache reuse
is not an owner approval or a quality verdict. The relation API has no persistent
verdict cache.

A rule evaluation baseline is `rules/<language>/<id>/baseline.json`. It records
accepted fixture answers and question identity for calibration/replay. It does
not accept findings in a user's project.

An accepted-findings baseline is a separate ledger, normally
`.jev-lint/accepted-findings.json`. It records explicit acceptance and counts;
changed model, policy or context requires rechecking. Missing or unobserved
subjects are not evidence of resolution. Acceptance never skips a model request.

The documentation record `.jev-lint/documents-baseline.json` contains recorded
comparisons for a content-digested documentation snapshot. Replay validates the
current snapshot and question identity; it does not produce a fresh model answer.

The Japanese terms 回答キャッシュ, ルール評価のbaseline, 指摘の受入台帳 and 文書比較の記録
name these respective concepts. Different translations are acceptable when the
same distinctions remain explicit.

target.quote:
## Accepted findings

Produce a [scan artifact](audit-api.md), then explicitly accept the current
findings with the operator's scope and immutable deployment identity:

```sh
jev-lint baseline write --artifact scan.json \
  --baseline .jev-lint/accepted-findings.json \
  --scope-id billing-contract --model-revision deployment-001

jev-lint baseline compare --artifact next-scan.json \
  --baseline .jev-lint/accepted-findings.json \
  --scope-id billing-contract --model-revision deployment-001

jev-lint baseline prune --artifact next-scan.json \
  --baseline .jev-lint/accepted-findings.json \
  --scope-id billing-contract --model-revision deployment-001
```

The ledger retains the accepting artifact digest, source SHA, run ID and
deployment identity. It stores fingerprints/counts rather than source quotes.
`write` is an explicit acceptance operation: use the owner approval store in a
hosted integration. Never let PR-controlled configuration accept its own findings.
`compare` is read-only and does not skip any model requests upstream.

Continuity keys track a scan's rule, path and exact subject text without line
numbers. Counts distinguish duplicate copies. Relation continuity uses the claim
ID, relation ID and target paths; callers should supply stable logical relation
IDs. Automatically discovered IDs can change when source ranges change.

An independent fingerprint binds the whole judged context, rule/cutoff, policy,
model and deployment identity. A matching finding is `accepted`; a new copy is
`new`; changed judgment inputs under the same continuity key are `recheck`.
Line movement alone does not change the continuity key, but a changed full request
context still requires rechecking. This is deliberately stricter than a line-only
suppression. Significant whitespace inside evidence is never normalized away.

`resolved` requires an explicit usable clean answer with the same acceptance
fingerprint. Missing answers, absent subjects, changed-context clean answers and
comparisons outside the observed set remain `unassessed`. A rewritten or removed
subject is not automatically proof that its defect was fixed. Its old ledger
entry remains until the operator replaces the accepted set. `prune` removes only
explicit resolutions, never adds entries, and refuses incomplete reviews.

Exact still-reported copies consume their allowance before clean duplicates, so
input order cannot accidentally prune a surviving finding. `write` and `prune`
validate before an atomic file replacement; they refuse known verdict-cache and
rule-baseline paths, and do not overwrite a file of another schema.

`compare` exits 1 for new/recheck findings, 3 for incomplete processing, and 0 when
the assessed scope has no new/recheck findings. Unobserved old entries stay in the
output even when that selected-scope comparison exits 0. The output always keeps
`qualityVerdict: "UNREVIEWED"`. Exit 2 is invalid input/configuration. A deployment
identity is required even for an offline CLI comparison; it is supplied by the
operator, not inferred from a moving model alias.

For relations, pass `--relation-input final-input.json` from the trusted dispatcher.
If the producer used a diff or planning budget, also pass
`--relation-options trusted-plan-options.json` with its `changedPaths`, `baseSha`,
`maxRelations` and/or `maxContextChars`. The existing report validator checks the
expected input/plan, source quotations and coverage. Unresolved owner decisions
remain unassessed and cannot be accepted as a complete review.

candidates.topic: Scope completion is separate from quality approval

reference.quote:
## Completion and quality

`complete` describes processing of the declared scope. A completed relation or
document comparison can contain contradictions. Zero candidates is not proof
that every possible defect was examined. Missing answers, relevant insufficient
context and deferred work remain visible.

`UNREVIEWED` means screening has not completed an independent quality review.
A finding is a candidate for review, not permission to modify, approve or merge.
Successful SARIF execution also does not imply quality PASS.

In Japanese, 処理完了 or 比較完了 can translate scope completion; 品質合格 means a
different assertion and cannot replace it.

target.quote:
## CLI

```sh
jev-lint scan src --no-config --cache none \
  --repository owner/project --run-id run-00001 --namespace account-001 \
  --policy-ref <approved-commit-sha> > scan.json
```

`scan` writes one JSON document. Exit `0` means the selected scope was completely
processed, including when it produced candidates. Exit `3` means partial or
failed processing; exit `2` is invalid configuration or source provenance.
It does not certify that a repository is correct or authorize a merge.

The default scan cache is disabled. An explicit cache path must be outside the
source checkout and requires `--model-revision <immutable-deployment-id>`.
`--source-sha` defaults to HEAD; `--max-candidates` limits the output and records
omissions as a partial scan. `--dry-run` also produces a partial scan, since no
new verdicts were obtained.

The source checkout must be clean, at the requested SHA, and owned by the trusted
dispatcher. Make it read-only while a scan is running. The API checks the
checkout before and after processing; these checks are not a sandbox against
another process that can mutate and restore files between checks. Do not install
dependencies, run lifecycle scripts, or load branch-controlled parser libraries
in this runner. Supply trusted rules explicitly to the API. CLI users should
also supply trusted configuration or use `--no-config` with packaged rules.

`complete` describes processing of the declared scope. A completed relation or

that every possible defect was examined. Missing answers, relevant insufficient
context and deferred work remain visible.

`UNREVIEWED` means screening has not completed an independent quality review.
A finding is a candidate for review, not permission to modify, approve or merge.
Successful SARIF execution also does not imply quality PASS.

In Japanese, 処理完了 or 比較完了 can translate scope completion; 品質合格 means a
different assertion and cannot replace it.

target.quote:
## SARIF

```sh
jev-lint check src --sarif > results.sarif
jev-lint review --base main --format sarif > results.sarif
jev-lint report --artifact scan.json --sarif --output results.sarif
jev-lint report --artifact relations.json --relation-input final-input.json \
  --relation-options trusted-plan-options.json --sarif --output relations.sarif
```

The exporter emits SARIF 2.1.0 with encoded repository-relative URIs and positive
line ranges. Incomplete reviews carry an unsuccessful execution and a fixed
notification instead of silently looking complete. No-verdict observations are
notes. The run's quality verdict remains UNREVIEWED even if execution succeeded.

Relation exports retain pinned related locations. Historical revisions are logical
locations with their SHA, so their old line ranges are not presented as current
head locations. A historical-only comparison can have no physical primary
location. Full source quotes are not embedded by the SARIF exporter, but finding
messages and file names can still be private; choose the destination accordingly.
Do not treat SARIF as the authenticated audit artifact or the watchpoint gate.

SARIF is available for check/review, scan and compatible replay results. Commit
subjects and plans require JSON because they are not current source locations.
All normalized review, acceptance, scope and SARIF APIs are also available through
the `jev-lint/review-artifact`, `/acceptance`, `/scope`, `/doctor`, and `/sarif`
package exports. Structural parsers do not authenticate the artifact's writer;
the integration must bind expected repository, snapshot, approval and access.

See the [evaluation record](../experiments/adoption/README.md) and
[upstream attribution](../THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md).

## Evidence and snapshots

Audit scan and relation source revisions are immutable git commits. A context
hash identifies the supplied request evidence; it is not a tenant access control
or an authenticated writer identity. Approval metadata comes from the owner
store, not from claims embedded in reviewed text.

Documentation checking can read a working tree. Such a snapshot uses content
digests and exact quoted ranges; its digest is not represented as a git commit.
An old document's line range must retain its old revision rather than being
presented as a current-head physical location.

target.quote:
## Bounded context retrieval

After a grounded comparison answers `insufficient_context`, the workflow searches
the catalog for same-file definitions and explicit relative named imports. It
supports import aliases and follows another dependency layer on the next round.
The import declaration itself is supplied with an imported body so the model can
verify the alias binding. Every addition is an exact quote from a pinned source.

Ambiguous module paths and duplicate same-name definitions are not guessed.
Dynamic imports, namespace/default imports, re-exports, computed dispatch and
non-JavaScript module resolution require caller-supplied context. The graph is
approximate; only the model evaluates whether the supplied behavior satisfies a
requirement. Retrieval does not execute code or add files outside the supplied
source catalog. Include permitted helper sources in the dispatcher manifest.

The default budgets are two retrieval rounds after the initial scan, 24,000 added
characters and 20 added excerpts across the workflow. There is also the relation
API's 20-context-excerpt limit per relation and its planned context-size limit.
No budget silently truncates an excerpt. Unresolved comparisons remain partial;
deferred discovery or context also keeps the workflow partial. Each round scans
the selected set again, so unchanged comparisons can incur another request.

## Evidence and snapshots

Audit scan and relation source revisions are immutable git commits. A context
hash identifies the supplied request evidence; it is not a tenant access control
or an authenticated writer identity. Approval metadata comes from the owner
store, not from claims embedded in reviewed text.

Documentation checking can read a working tree. Such a snapshot uses content
digests and exact quoted ranges; its digest is not represented as a git commit.
An old document's line range must retain its old revision rather than being

target.quote:
## Live and replay

A live check reads regular files from the working tree, refuses symlink sources
and records content digests. It does not execute checkout scripts or load parser
libraries. The transport checks snapshot freshness before sending and the runner
checks it again after evaluation. Supply a trusted manifest in a hosted service;
repository text is evidence and cannot approve itself. Credentials stay in the
environment and are not document inputs.

`--dry-run` prints the plan with zero model requests. `--record` writes all
answers, locations, question identity, usage and omissions. The default bounds
are 100 comparisons, 64,000 characters per comparison, 256 kB per source file
and two million characters of loaded source text. Actual requests also have
client-wide request, token, time and cost bounds.

Replay validates recorded answers against the current manifest, source digests,
selected excerpts and question. It makes no model requests. Any changed input
requires refreshing the record; stale evidence cannot certify the new snapshot.
CI checks generated facts and replays the committed documentation record without
an API key. A changed documentation binding therefore needs a new live record.

Exit 1 means a contradiction was found, 3 means incomplete/stale assessment,
and 2 means invalid arguments or manifest. Exit 0 means the declared comparisons
agreed; it does not certify all documentation or quality PASS. Snapshot changes
during a run take precedence over an old contradiction and yield exit 3.
Every report retains `qualityVerdict: "UNREVIEWED"`.

reference.quote:
## Documentation consistency

`jev-lint docs` compares explicit claims, glossary definitions and translations,
retaining both source locations. This repository checks its own README pair,
API guides and contributor instructions against generated project facts and
canonical terminology.

```sh
jev-lint docs --dry-run
jev-lint docs --record .jev-lint/documents-baseline.json
jev-lint docs --replay .jev-lint/documents-baseline.json
```

The manifest is `.jev-lint/documents.json`; `--document-manifest` selects another.
Replay is offline and rejects changed sources or questions. Contradictions exit 1;
incomplete or stale assessments exit 3. The report remains `UNREVIEWED`.
See the [self-check guide](docs/self-check.md) for scope, budgets and evaluation.

target.quote:
## ドキュメントの整合性

`jev-lint docs` は、明示した主張、用語の定義、翻訳の意味を比較し、両方の出典位置を残す。
このリポジトリでは日英README、APIガイド、開発者向け指示を、生成したプロジェクト情報と
共通の用語定義に照らして検査する。

```sh
jev-lint docs --dry-run
jev-lint docs --record .jev-lint/documents-baseline.json
jev-lint docs --replay .jev-lint/documents-baseline.json
```

定義ファイルは `.jev-lint/documents.json`。`--document-manifest` で別のものを指定できる。
再生には通信が不要で、出典や質問が変わっていれば拒否する。不一致は終了コード1、
未評価・古い記録は3になる。結果の品質判定は `UNREVIEWED` のまま。
対象範囲、予算、評価方法は[自己検査ガイド](docs/self-check.md)にある。
